IR.rationale: Trend followers typically carry long-duration bond positions built up in a falling-yield environment. A jump in intermediate yields relative to the policy rate marks a bond sell-off that reverses these positions and drags on returns.

B.rationale: Widening spreads together with weak high-yield returns mark a deteriorating credit state. Such states tend to develop into persistent cross-asset risk-off trends that time-series momentum strategies monetise (the 'crisis alpha' pattern).

V.rationale: CTA payoffs resemble long lookback straddles (Fung-Hsieh). Elevated implied volatility signals large directional moves, which are the environment in which trend following earns.

AP.rationale: Broad weakness in both US and EM equities is the global risk-off state. In that state the convex, often short-equity positioning of trend followers tends to pay.

ST.rationale: Cross-sectional equity momentum and time-series momentum across futures share a common trend-persistence component. A strong momentum factor therefore indicates a trending environment.

FX.rationale: Broad dollar moves are among the most persistent macro trends and a large share of CTA risk. A strengthening dollar describes the state of the main FX trend.

COM.rationale: Broad commodity moves are a core component of managed-futures books. The direction of the commodity complex summarises the trend state of that sleeve.

MC.rationale: Rising systemic financial stress coincides with sustained deleveraging trends across asset classes. Historically this is where managed futures deliver positive convexity.

ENDG.rationale: Strategy returns show mild persistence because the underlying market trends persist. Recent strong performance signals an ongoing trending regime.

IR.rationale: Rate shocks raise bond-futures volatility. Fixed income is the largest risk allocation of most CTAs, so these shocks transmit into index variance beyond what its own past variance predicts.

B.rationale: Credit spread widening signals rising aggregate risk and a coming increase in cross-asset volatility.

V.rationale: CTA variance reflects volatility across many asset classes. Joint high equity and gold implied volatility indicates broad, cross-asset uncertainty rather than an equity-specific episode.

AP.rationale: Negative equity returns are followed by higher volatility (the leverage and volatility-feedback effects). This spills over to the futures markets that CTAs trade.

ST.rationale: Weak momentum returns indicate trend reversals and momentum-crash conditions. These are associated with turbulent, high-variance trend-follower returns.

FX.rationale: Yen appreciation is the classic signature of carry unwinds and flight to safety. Such episodes bring abrupt cross-asset moves and higher variance.

COM.rationale: Commodity sell-offs tend to be accompanied by rising commodity volatility, a component of CTA risk.

MC.rationale: Elevated financial stress indexes predict higher future market volatility across asset classes.

ENDG.rationale: Very high recent variance tends to mean-revert faster than a simple persistence model implies. Its level is therefore informative about the residual.

IR.rationale: Sharp bond sell-offs abruptly reverse the long-duration trend positions CTAs commonly hold. This is a frequent source of their worst weeks.

B.rationale: A sharp credit rally with tightening spreads marks a risk-on rebound. Such rebounds catch trend followers positioned for continued stress.

V.rationale: High implied volatility widens the distribution of outcomes for convex trend strategies. It raises the chance of tail outcomes, including losses from whipsaws.

AP.rationale: Strong broad equity rallies, especially after declines, are the setting of momentum crashes. Short or underweight trend positions suffer most there (Daniel-Moskowitz).

ST.rationale: Momentum losses combined with strong short-term reversal indicate a market reversal regime. That regime is hostile to trend persistence.

FX.rationale: A sudden dollar reversal cuts against one of the most persistent and heavily held CTA trends.

COM.rationale: Sharp commodity rebounds squeeze the short commodity trend positions that build up during declining markets.

MC.rationale: Stressed conditions bring policy interventions and abrupt reversals that can produce large trend-follower drawdowns.

ENDG.rationale: After unusually strong recent performance, positions are extended and crowded. This raises the risk of a sharp reversal loss.

IR.rationale: Falling intermediate yields relative to the policy rate mark flight-to-quality bond rallies. These deliver large gains to long-duration trend positions.

B.rationale: Persistent credit deterioration develops into sustained risk-off trends. These are where managed futures historically post their largest gains.

V.rationale: The straddle-like payoff of trend following earns most when realised moves are large. Elevated implied volatility anticipates such moves.

AP.rationale: Equity sell-offs are the classic 'crisis alpha' setting in which CTAs' convex positioning produces outsized gains.

ST.rationale: Strong momentum returns indicate a persistent trending environment that supports large trend-following profits.

FX.rationale: Strong dollar trends, often accompanying global risk-off phases, are a major source of big CTA gains.

COM.rationale: Extended commodity declines have historically produced large profits on short commodity trend positions.

MC.rationale: Tightening financial conditions accompany broad deleveraging trends across asset classes, which trend followers capture.

ENDG.rationale: Strong recent performance indicates an established trend regime that tends to persist over the next weeks.
